title: Born in Toronto in 1912; mother, step-fathers and mining towns
summary: Gil gives his birth date and place, then describes his wandering mother, her several husbands and a childhood in mining and lumber towns.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: There are of course such fundamental things that are very familiar to you but that other people years and years later will want to know about. I happen to know that you somehow made your way into the United States from Canada. Do you want to go back to Canada and talk about your background there and family and that sort of thing as much as you want? You were born in Canada weren't you?
Yes, I was, yes.
Where specifically?
Toronto.
And when?
And you stayed there in school until when? Were you a kind of drop-out in the days when they weren't using the word?
No.
No, oh.
I started school when I was eight at Nelson British (NelsonBridge, Columbia?).
At where, NelsonBridge
Then we came to (Spokane) Washington.
Now when you say 'we'?
My mother.
Your mother. What about your father?
Well my father is dead. But I had some step-fathers. Mama was married five times.
(LAUGHTER). I was quite fascinated by you saying some step-fathers. (LAUGHTER).
Well I had some brothers and sisters which I never knew because they were born before me and a couple of them died before I was born. (Mother was about 45 before I was born?).
Well, was she in show business or..... No?
No, she just had the wanderlust. Worked her way across
Canada into Washington, Idaho. And my step-father was a miner, so we lived in Idaho and Montana, Washington and Oregon and California in mining towns. And my mother was, let's see, she cooked mostly.
She'd answer an ad in the paper for..... ......
In restaurants or private homes or what? Private homes?
In private homes usually on a farm. I remember a farm and lumber camps and things like that.

And we did that until we moved to Stockton I think. Then my mother became a cook, really; she still cooked but she took care of children more then than she had before. Before that she was a cook mainly. She did have some (unintelligible)
She would have to be up at three o'clock in the morning to get the thing started before they all came into the beanary to eat. The wagons the (unintelligible ?). It was that kind of a life.
Which hardly seems
conducive to the kind of person that you finally became. When did you then first notice the spark of the .........
In highschool.
In highschool which was where?
In Berkeley. There's where I first knew .........
You just really didn't realise that you were musically inclined before that?
My mother had a mandolin that she'd play and she used to carry around with her. But .........
And you didn't pay much attention even to that did you say?
No.
Well does this suggest then that something of the spark of your musicality came from your mother? Did you know anything about any particular talent your father had?
No. Just that (Unintelligible - inaudible)
Oh those were the days
when the mandolin and banjo was a popular home instrument, yes. And just about everybody was trying to work out a fret or two, huh?
(LAUGHTER).
The music is the same as it is now. A lot of the Country Western music is Now its electric, but the same. The style and sound of the singers and lots of the sounds are almost the same.
